posts.text:
Danny Almonte threw a perfect game at the Little League World Series, struck out 16 of 18 batters, and got the key to New York City. He was supposed to be 12. Years later he said it on camera: he knew he wasn’t playing kids his age. He said what the adults told him to say.

August 18, 2001. A left-hander from the Bronx faced 18 kids in Williamsport and struck out 16 of them. Perfect game.

By the end of the tournament he had struck out 62 of the 72 batters he faced and allowed three hits.

His team, the Rolando Paulino All-Stars, became the Baby Bombers. They finished third. New York gave them a parade, a tribute at Yankee Stadium and the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange.

On August 28, Mayor Rudy Giuliani handed them the keys to the city and declared it Rolando Paulino All-Stars Day.

Parents from a rival team had already paid a private investigator $10,000 to prove the ages were fake. He came up empty.

Sports Illustrated went to the civil records office in Moca, Dominican Republic. In the ledger: in 1994, his father had registered Danny’s birth as April 7, 1987. He was 14.

The certificate that said 1989 had only been registered in 2000, the year he moved to the Bronx.

Within three days of the key to the city, Little League stripped every win. His father and the league’s founder, Rolando Paulino, were banned for life. Dominican prosecutors charged his father with falsifying the certificate.

Even President Bush weighed in. He said he was extremely disappointed that adults would try to fudge the boy’s age.

Danny didn’t speak English. He was cleared of wrongdoing.

Years later, in an ESPN short film, he told his side. He knew he wasn’t playing with kids his age. When he asked, he was told to say he was 12. When your dad tells you something, he says, you do it. At that age you say what your parents want you to say.

He wishes it never happened.

The adults got lifetime bans from a youth league. The kid got his perfect game erased from the record book, and his name became the punchline every time a Little Leaguer looks too big.

So who really cheated in Williamsport? The 14-year-old on the mound, or the grown men holding his paperwork?

America’s economy faces a growing problem: not enough people, per Business Insider.

The US population grew by just 1.8 million people in 2025, down from 3.2 million the year before, per the Census Bureau. Immigration accounted for the entire slowdown. 

Net immigration is projected to fall to about 321,000 this year, far below the low-immigration scenario Census previously modeled.
